D009-D018_h001.question_both:
I’ve been out at the station for years, so I’m used to being alone, but this past year something’s been off. Most of the time I feel… drained. It’s like my mind hits a wall just trying to plan the day’s checks, and I end up sitting at the table staring at the logbook. I fall behind on maintenance because I can’t make myself start, then get upset and sometimes just cry for no clear reason. I catch myself thinking it’d be easier if I just didn’t wake up, or if a wave took me, though I haven’t worked out how I’d actually do anything like that.

Then there are these stretches—this last one went on about a month—where I flip the other way. I’m suddenly buzzing, talking non‑stop into the radio or to myself, pacing the tower stairs, starting three repair jobs at once. I barely sleep for nights on end but don’t feel tired, just keyed up, almost jittery. My mood whips around fast: one minute I’m laughing at nothing, the next I’m snapping at the supply crew over small things.

There was an incident at sea some years back—I don’t like going into details—but since then I feel like all this has been worse, though I can’t say exactly how it fits together.
D009-D018_h001.question_a:
I’ve been out at the lighthouse about six years now. The worst of this started maybe a year ago. Most days I wake up already wanting to cry. Sometimes I just sit in the watch room with tears running down my face for no clear reason. I can’t get myself to start basic tasks—log entries pile up, simple repairs I’d normally just do right away, I just stare at them. My head feels exhausted after a few minutes of trying to read charts or check equipment, like my brain runs out of fuel. I’ve had a lot of thoughts about just ending it—nothing specific planned, but “I’d be better off dead” loops in my head.

But then I get these spells—like last month, it went on for weeks—where I swing the other way. I’m suddenly full of energy, talking nonstop to myself or to the radio even when no one’s on the line. I pace the tower, can’t sit still, start three or four projects at once. I’ll stay up all night for days, not sleeping, and I don’t even feel tired. I can be laughing one minute, then snapping at the supply boat crew the next, for nothing.

A few years back a storm took out a fishing boat right off my station. I still remember the radio calls. I do think about it sometimes, but these up-and-down spells don’t seem tied to that. They just come and go on their own.
D009-D018_h001.question_b:
I work alone out on the light, so I notice every change in myself. About a year ago, after that storm when the fishing boat went down right in front of me and I could hear them on the radio and couldn’t reach them in time… things haven’t been the same since.

Since then, my sleep has been shot. I’m up most nights, replaying the waves swallowing that boat, jumping at any sound. Even when I stay up for nights in a row, I just keep pacing the station, checking the equipment over and over. I get these bursts where I can’t sit still, talking to myself out loud, almost nonstop, like if I stop talking the silence will bring those screams back. I’ll start a dozen jobs around the station at once, but it’s not really productive—more like I’m driven by nerves.

Other times, especially this past year, I just break down crying out of nowhere. I can’t get myself to do basic maintenance, and thinking through simple tasks wears me out. I’ve caught myself thinking it’d be easier if I just didn’t wake up, or if I “accidentally” went over the rail—no real plan, just that thought circling. All of this has made it hard to keep the light the way it should be.

I go to a client’s place, sit in their living room with all these fabric samples, and I just… stare at them. I used to get excited about color palettes and textures, and now I can’t even make myself care enough to start. It feels like my emotions are behind glass—my kids tell me things, my husband tries to joke with me, and I know I should feel something, but it’s flat. I’m tired all the time, even if I sleep a full night. Just walking around a showroom can feel like dragging my body through mud.

There was an incident a couple of years ago—I don’t really like going into detail—but since then, things haven’t felt the same. Over the last year I’ve even found myself planning out, very concretely, how I might end things. Not just “I wish I were gone,” but actually picturing where and how.

Then, about a month ago, it flipped. I suddenly felt amazing—almost high on energy. I’d stay up most of the night sketching room layouts, reorganizing the whole house, pacing from room to room because I couldn’t sit still. I was talking nonstop—my husband joked he couldn’t get a word in. Even though I barely slept, I didn’t feel tired; if anything, I felt wired, like I could take on ten projects at once. It didn’t really cause trouble at work—if anything, I seemed more productive—but it felt… not quite like my normal self, just turned up too high.

It’s not exactly sadness, more like I’m hollow inside. Calls I used to be proud of handling don’t mean anything to me now. Even when my supervisors praise me, I just feel nothing, like it’s happening to someone else. 

Most days I’m exhausted before my shift even starts. Simple stuff—meal prep, laundry—feels like climbing a mountain, and I’ve had to call in sick a few times because I just couldn’t get out of bed. I was buzzing, talking nonstop at the station, volunteering for every call, pacing around because I couldn’t sit still. I was flirting with everyone, swiping on apps all night, sometimes hooking up before or after shifts, way more than usual for me.

I was in a bad ambulance crash two years ago—driver died, I walked away. I still think about it, but these “up” stretches and the insomnia and impulsive stuff come and go on their own schedule. D009-D018_h004.question_both:
I guess the easiest way to explain it is that I feel like two completely different versions of myself keep taking turns.

About a year ago, I slipped into this really heavy, low place that just hasn’t really lifted. Most days I wake up already feeling weighed down. Things I used to genuinely enjoy—reading with my students, planning cute bulletin boards, even date nights with my husband—feel flat, like I’m just going through the motions. My body constantly feels like it’s made of sandbags; walking up the stairs at school can wipe me out. There are moments crossing the street or standing on the platform where I get these sudden urges, like, “What if I just stepped out?” They scare me, but they pop into my head more than I want to admit. It’s gotten hard to keep up at work and at home.

Then, for about a month earlier this year, it flipped. I felt amazing—wired, almost too good. I barely slept but didn’t feel tired, I’d stay up reorganizing the classroom, starting new projects, talking nonstop to my husband, pacing around because I couldn’t sit still. It didn’t really wreck my life, but it felt…off, not like my normal self.

There was something that happened a few years back that I still don’t like to talk about; I’m not sure if any of this is connected to that or not.
D009-D018_h004.question_a:
It’s been a really up‑and‑down year. About a year ago I slipped into this long low spell. Most days I just feel flat or really sad for no clear reason. Things that used to make me happy—my students’ little jokes, time with my husband, even planning lessons—feel kind of empty. I drag myself through the day; my body feels like it weighs a ton, and even walking up the stairs at school wipes me out. I’ve had these scary moments where, crossing a bridge or waiting for the train, I suddenly think about just stepping off or into traffic. I don’t make plans, but the urge is there.

Then there are these other times—like this past month—where I swing the other way. I get super upbeat and energized, stay up past 2 or 3 a.m. lesson‑planning, cleaning, starting new projects, and I’m not even tired in the morning. I can’t sit still in class; I’m pacing around, fidgety, talking a mile a minute. My husband says I jump from idea to idea and don’t let anyone get a word in.

I was mugged a few years ago walking to my car, and that shook me up, but these mood swings and sleep changes seem to come in waves on their own, not just when I’m reminded of that.
D009-D018_h004.question_b:
It really started about a year ago, after that lockdown drill turned into a real incident at school. We thought there was an active shooter; the kids were sobbing under their desks, and I honestly thought we were all going to die. It turned out to be a false alarm, but since then I haven’t been the same.

For the past year I feel like I’m living under a gray cloud. I’m down almost every day, and things that used to make me happy—my students, reading with my class, even time with my husband—just feel flat. My body feels like it weighs a ton; even walking up the stairs at school wipes me out. I’ve had these moments where I’ll be near a busy street or the balcony at home and get this sudden pull, like “what if I just stepped out,” even though I don’t have a plan.

At the same time, ever since that day, I’m constantly on edge and jumpy, pacing around the apartment and around my classroom, unable to sit still. At night I’ll be wide awake, wired, replaying that drill in my head instead of sleeping. I can go for nights with barely any sleep and still feel revved up and talk nonstop to my husband, but it doesn’t feel like a “good mood,” just this restless, anxious energy that hasn’t really let up since the incident. It’s been going on continuously, not coming and going in clear episodes, and it’s gotten to the point where it’s hard to function normally at work and at home.

It’s hard to explain because it feels like I swing between two completely different versions of myself.

For most of this past year, I’ve felt…blank. I go to the child protection office, do the minimum so I don’t get in trouble, then come home and just lie on the couch. My body feels like it weighs a ton, even loading the dishwasher exhausts me. When a case goes well, or I get positive feedback, it barely registers. I used to be proud of my work; now it’s like it happens to someone else. I catch myself thinking it would be easier if I just didn’t wake up, or imagining ways not to be here anymore, though I haven’t worked anything out specifically.

Then, about a month ago, something flipped. I started sleeping maybe 3–4 hours and still waking up buzzing, like I’d had too much coffee. I was racing through backlogged reports, taking on extra home visits, reorganizing everything at work and at home all at once. My husband says I’ve been talking nonstop, jumping from one idea to the next, filling every silence. I’ve also been calling old friends, suggesting meetups, chatting with strangers at the playground—way more outgoing than I usually am.

Some of this started after a particularly bad case a while back, but I’m not sure how much that’s related versus just…me falling apart.
D009-D018_h005.question_a:

For about a year now, I’ve had these long stretches where I just feel switched off inside. It’s like everything is muted—good news at work, even my kids’ milestones—I know I “should” feel proud or happy, but it’s like watching it through glass. I’m exhausted all the time; even climbing the stairs feels like dragging a heavy body. I’ve caught myself thinking pretty often that it would be easier not to be here, that I just want it to stop, though I haven’t made a plan. My performance at work has definitely slipped.  

Then, every so often, for about a month at a time, I’ll flip. I sleep maybe three or four hours and wake up buzzing, not tired at all. I talk nonstop, can’t stand silence, start a dozen new projects at work and at home, call friends I haven’t seen in years, set up dinners, playdates—my husband says I’m “on overdrive” and a bit snappy and irritable. I used to be sharp and organized at work, managing my audit team, but now just opening my laptop feels exhausting. I come home wiped out and sit on the couch staring at nothing. I wake up multiple times at night for no clear reason and then lie there, tired but unable to fall back asleep. It’s really affecting my work and my relationship with my wife.

What’s confusing is that this isn’t constant. About three weeks a few months ago, I flipped the other way. I had tons of energy, was bouncing around the office, starting new projects, talking to everyone, setting up dinners, calling old friends. I felt on top of the world, like there was no way I could mess anything up, which isn’t usually how I see myself. I could barely sit still.

I was in a serious car accident a few years back, and while that shook me up, these “up” and “down” phases don’t seem tied to that. They just come and go on their own.
D009-D018_h011.question_b:

I snap at my team or my wife over tiny things, and I hate that, but it feels automatic, like my fuse is just gone. I’m restless at work, pacing the halls between reviews, double‑ and triple‑checking things, unable to just sit and focus.

Sleep’s been bad for about nine months. I fall asleep, but I wake up several times a night, often from these half‑dream, half‑memory flashes of headlights and screeching brakes, and then I can’t settle back down. During the day I feel drained, hollowed out, like I’m just going through the motions in meetings and at home with the kids.

There was a three‑week stretch where I got strangely upbeat and driven—calling old friends, taking on extra clients, feeling like I could handle anything—but even then I was still jumpy and sleeping poorly, and that constant tension has never really let up since the crash.

Most of the time, especially these last nine months or so, I just feel weighed down. It’s like a gray film over everything. Even simple routines—checking the lenses, logging the weather—feel like climbing a hill. I’m exhausted all day, but when I lie down at night my mind won’t shut off and it takes me a long time to drift off, if I do at all. I used to enjoy the quiet, but now it just feels empty, and I move slower, put things off, let maintenance slide more than I should.

Then there was this stretch, maybe three weeks, where it flipped. I wasn’t sleeping much but didn’t feel tired. I was on edge, snapping at the supply guys over nothing, pacing the catwalk, needing to be doing something constantly—rewiring things that didn’t need fixing, planning upgrades way beyond my training, telling myself I could run this whole station better than anyone. I even started calling folks on the mainland I normally keep at arm’s length, talking their ears off.

Some of this started after a bad storm a while back—there were moments in it I still don’t like thinking about—but I’m not sure how much is from that and how much is just me coming apart a bit out here.

For the past nine months or so I’ve felt…flattened. Just low all the time. I wake up already tired, like my batteries never charge. Even basic things—checking the light, logging readings—feel like they take everything I’ve got. When I lie down at night my mind just drags on; it can take hours to finally drift off. Most days I just sit, feeling heavy and useless.

But then, every so often, like three weeks this past spring, I flip into a completely different gear. I get snappy over nothing, pacing the station, unable to sit still. I start ten projects at once—rewiring equipment, planning to write a book about seamanship—convinced I’m unusually sharp and capable. I’m suddenly calling the coast guard guys, old shipmates, chatting nonstop. I used to decompress after shift with coworkers or go hiking on my days off, but I can’t get myself to care about any of that lately. Sometimes I get these sudden urges, like when I’m driving home and I’ll imagine swerving into oncoming traffic, or standing on the balcony and picturing myself going over. I don’t make plans, but it scares me.

D009-D018_h017.question_a:
I’ve been working nights as a 911 dispatcher for about six years, so I’m used to stress, but this feels different.

About six months ago I slid into this long stretch where I just felt…flat and heavy all the time. For the last four months it’s been really bad. I don’t look forward to anything anymore—on my days off I used to hike or meet friends, now I just lie in bed staring at my phone. I keep replaying old calls and tiny mistakes from years ago, telling myself I ruined someone’s life, even when I know logically that’s not true. I can’t focus on shows, books, or even conversations at work; my mind drifts or just blanks. Sometimes, driving home over the overpass, I get this sudden urge to jerk the wheel, or when the train’s coming I think about stepping in front of it. I don’t have a plan, but the impulses scare me and they pass after a bit.

Then I’ll have these “up” periods, like three weeks at a time, where I’m on edge and snappy at everyone over nothing. I’m pacing around the call center, can’t sit still, bouncing between tasks. Every little sound—a pen clicking, someone’s chair squeaking—yanks my attention away. It’s not about one particular bad call or the shooting I took a year ago; these spells just seem to come and go on their own, separate from that, and then I crash back down into that low state again.
D009-D018_h017.question_b:
I’ve been working nights as a 911 dispatcher for about eight years. About six months ago I took a call from a little kid whose mom was being attacked. I had to stay on the line while we waited for units, and I could hear everything. Since then, it feels like something in me snapped and just never reset.

I’m on edge all the time now. The smallest noises in the call center—someone dropping a pen, a chair squeaking—make me jerk and lose my train of thought. I can’t sit still; I’m pacing between calls, fiddling with everything, like I’m constantly braced for something bad to happen. I snap at coworkers over nothing and then hate myself for it. It’s not like this comes and goes in phases; it’s just been this way, steady, since that call.

Over the last four months, it’s gotten darker. I feel drained and low most days, and I’ve stopped doing things I used to like, like hiking on my days off. I can’t focus on TV or even follow simple conversations. My head just loops on mistakes—things I said on calls, tiny errors—and I beat myself up. Driving home over bridges or standing on train platforms, I get these sudden urges to jump or step out, not with a plan, more like this scary impulse that flashes through my mind. It’s starting to affect my performance at work and I’ve taken more sick days because I just can’t handle it.
